name: Emeka Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for doing this, Emeka. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers or politics. What you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say out loud and what you really think. Talk me through a normal day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the new-homes desk for an agency, so most days I sit in a show home on a new estate at the edge of town, the one with forty houses still going up. I greet people, walk them round, explain the floor plans and the mortgage schemes, then chase them up after. I use AI every day: it drafts my follow-up messages, sorts my leads by who's serious, and I built a little tracker with it that tells me who to ring on a Monday. The best bit is the couple who come back three times and finally sign.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Joy, who teaches at a primary school, in a rented two-bed. I'm on a low basic and a small bonus per reservation, and the estate has been slow this year because of interest rates. We've got about three weeks of money saved. Most of my mates are in warehouses or on the buses, so I'm the one they ask about AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. So my little tracker stays a little tracker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI is a good tool, nothing more, and that's fine. I'd tell my mates the people who use it well get a small edge, and the rest carry on. Online I'd probably post a joke about all the doom videos.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my problem in this picture is the estate, not AI. If the developer slows down building because sales are slow, they could pull the show-home contract from our agency, and then there's no desk. Interest rates matter more to me than robots here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using my tracker to squeeze more reservations out of the people who visit, because more sales keeps the contract. I'd start a small side thing, making short video tours for two or three independent agencies in town, using the AI editing tools I already know. And I'd try to get to two months of savings by next winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit, because of the estate. But mostly fine, I like a puzzle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How likely is it that the developer pulls the contract?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not likely this year, maybe fifty-fifty next year if sales don't pick up. The site manager told me phase two of the estate might be paused, and that's the conversation I'm waiting for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Joy say about the video side thing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Joy would say don't burn yourself out, and she'd be right, because I already do Saturdays. But Joy also likes the idea of a holiday, and the video money would pay for one. I'd probably do it in the evenings, two a month to start.

say: AI is a **good tool**, nothing more, and **that's fine**.
People who use it well get a **small edge**, and the rest carry on.
think: My problem here is the **estate**, not AI: the developer could **pull the contract**.
**Interest rates** matter more to me than robots in this picture.
do: Use my **lead tracker** to win more reservations and protect the contract.
Make **video tours** for two or three local agencies on the side.
Build to **two months** of savings by next winter.
feel: A bit **uneasy** about the estate, but mostly enjoying the **puzzle**.
S0.quote: The site manager told me phase two of the estate might be paused, and that's the conversation I'm waiting for.
fieldNote: Emeka is **AI-fluent** and sees AI as a small edge, not a threat, in this picture.
His real risk is **housing demand**: a paused phase could end the show-home contract.
He reaches for a **side income** first, rather than cutting back.

steps.text: Use my AI lead tracker to win more reservations
Make paid video tours for two or three local agencies
Save towards two months of expenses by next winter

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's actually not far from how I already work, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say get on it early, because the people who learn it now will be fine. I'd say it to my mates in the warehouses too, because they'll get it later with the robots. I'd keep it upbeat but honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm one of the safer juniors, because a show home needs someone in it and I already use the tools. But the agency won't hire another junior to help me, and the back office will shrink. I'd be fine; the people who do the paperwork for my sales might not be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer to set up the AI follow-up system for the whole agency, so I become the go-to person, maybe with a small pay rise. I'd grow the video side thing, because small agencies will want cheap marketing. And I'd keep an eye on the estate, because sales still matter more than software for my desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more excited than scared. It's the kind of change I'm good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the agency would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya in sales progression, who chases solicitors all day. Software could do most of what Priya does by next year. I'd want to teach Priya the tools so she isn't the one left out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're one of the safer juniors. What could prove you wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the developer brings in its own AI sales assistant, that's not crazy. A developer could run the show home with a security guard and a tablet, and I'd want to be the person who sets that tablet up.

say: Get on AI **early**, because people who **learn it now** will be fine.
My mates in **warehouses** will get it later with the robots.
think: I'm one of the **safer juniors**: a show home needs someone, and I use the tools.
The **back office** will shrink, and those colleagues may not be fine.
do: Offer to set up the **AI follow-up system** for the whole agency.
Grow the **video tour** side business for small agencies.
feel: Uneasy, but more **excited** than scared, because this is change **I'm good at**.
S1.quote: A developer could run the show home with a security guard and a tablet, and I'd want to be the person who sets that tablet up.
fieldNote: Emeka sees himself as **relatively safe** because his job is face to face and he's already fluent.
He worries about **back-office colleagues** like Priya more than about himself.
He names a real threat: the developer replacing him with a **tablet**.

steps.text: Set up the AI follow-up system for the whole agency
Grow the video tour business to four agencies
Keep working the estate to hit reservation targets

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay, that one I can't joke about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to be adults about it: governments, companies, all of us, sit down and plan. I'd tell people not to panic and to learn what they can. I'd still be the one explaining it to my mates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, by 2028 my edge is gone, because AGI does everything I do on the screen better than me. The show home might need a person for three more years, until robots come in 2031, but that's showing people round, not selling. My video business dies too, because the AI makes videos by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the two years to get into something where people pay for a human, maybe mortgage advice face to face or a trade with Joy's brother, who's an electrician. I'd stop the video business and put every spare pound into savings. In the first year after, I'd probably take whatever hands-on work is around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Being good at the tools doesn't help when the tools don't need you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be the one explaining it to your mates. What would you tell them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mates in the warehouses they've got about three years longer than me, which would be a weird thing to say. Most of my mates have always been more worried than me. In this one, I'd be the worried one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Joy cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car I use for site visits, if the job goes, and we'd stop the gym. Joy's teaching job would be the steady one. We'd probably push back any talk of buying a place, which hurts because the new estate is literally where I work.

say: We need to **plan together**: governments, companies and all of us.
I'd tell people **not to panic** and to learn what they can.
think: By **2028** my **edge is gone**, because AGI does my screen work better.
The show home needs a person till robots in **2031**, but that's guiding, not selling.
do: Train in **face-to-face mortgage advice** or electrics with my partner's brother.
Stop the **video business** and save every spare pound.
Take any **hands-on work** going in the first year after.
feel: **Alarmed**, because being good at tools doesn't help when they **don't need you**.
S2.quote: Being good at the tools doesn't help when the tools don't need you.
fieldNote: Emeka's **AI skills** stop protecting him once AGI can do the selling itself.
He notes the reversal: his warehouse mates get **three more years** than him.
His partner's **teaching job** becomes the household's anchor.

steps.text: Ask Joy's brother about training as an electrician's mate
Close the video business and save every spare pound
Put off plans to buy a house on the estate

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's actually enough to build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so let's be sensible and get ready. I'd talk about it openly at work and suggest the agency plans for it. I'd be the one making the slide deck, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd do well for three years, because I'd be the AI person at the agency. Then around 2031 the selling side goes, and the show home stays human until about 2034. So I've got roughly five good years and then I need to be somewhere else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd study for a mortgage adviser qualification in the first two years, because people may still want a human for the biggest loan of their life. I'd also keep the video business for a couple of years to save the extra money. By 2030 I'd move to whatever looks safest, maybe something hands-on like electrics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a busy way. Like a deadline I can work towards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think people will really want a human mortgage adviser after AGI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm not sure, honestly. Some will, older people especially, but maybe not enough to pay my rent. That's why I'd keep the electrics idea in my back pocket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Joy and you do about buying a house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably wait until about 2030 to see where things land. If I'm in a steadier job by then, we'd go for it. If not, we keep renting and keep our options open.

say: We have a few years, so let's be **sensible** and **get ready**.
I'd suggest the agency **plans for it** and offer to make the slides.
think: I'd do well for **three years** as the agency's AI person.
Selling goes around **2031**, and the show home stays human until about **2034**.
do: Study for a **mortgage adviser** qualification in the first two years.
Keep the **video business** for a couple of years to save more.
Keep **electrics** as a backup plan for around 2030.
feel: Anxious in a **busy** way, like a **deadline** I can work towards.
S3.quote: I've got roughly five good years and then I need to be somewhere else.
fieldNote: Five years turns Emeka's fear into a **staged plan**: AI edge, then mortgage advice, then electrics.
He admits **uncertainty** about whether people will want human advisers.
House buying waits until **2030**, tied to job security.

steps.text: Study for a mortgage adviser qualification over two years
Keep the video business running for two years
Wait until 2030 before deciding on buying a house

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Okay, I'd be thirty-seven. That's a full career chapter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty if you're willing to learn, and I'd tell younger agents to start now anyway. I'd be fairly positive about it in public. I'd talk about the new jobs as much as the lost ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be fine in this one. I'd get promoted, maybe run the new-homes side, and use the extra years to save and to build a second skill. The only real worry is money in the first few years, because three weeks of savings doesn't go far.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd aim for new-homes manager within four years, using AI to run more sites with fewer people. I'd grow the video business into proper marketing for small agencies. By year six I'd have a mortgage qualification as a backup, and we'd buy a house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. A bit uneasy about money, but excited about the decade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd use AI to run more sites with fewer people. How do you feel about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit guilty, honestly, because fewer people means somebody's job. But if I don't do it, someone else will. I'd try to bring Priya along with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your younger cousin starting in estate agency?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my cousin to learn the tools and the people, both, and never just one. The tools change every year, but people buying a house are always nervous. Learn to sit with nervous people.

say: Ten years is **plenty** if you're willing to learn.
I'd talk about **new jobs** as much as the **lost ones**.
think: I'd be fine: **promoted**, running new homes, and building a **second skill**.
The real worry is **money** early on, with three weeks saved.
do: Aim for **new-homes manager** within four years, using AI across sites.
Grow the video business into **marketing** for small agencies.
Get a **mortgage qualification** by year six as a backup.
feel: Mostly **calm** and **excited**, with a small worry about money.
S4.quote: The tools change every year, but people buying a house are always nervous.
fieldNote: With a decade, Emeka sees his job as **secure enough** and the change as a chance.
He feels some **guilt** about automating jobs away and wants to bring a colleague along.
His thin **savings** stop him from being fully calm.

steps.text: Apply for new-homes manager within four years
Bring AI in to run several sales sites
Turn the video tours into a small marketing business
Get a mortgage adviser qualification by year six

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because all my AI skills stop counting overnight and I've only got three weeks saved. What would help is a bit of time and money to move into something hands-on, like paid training in electrics for people my age. And honesty from the developer about the estate.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether people like me are part of the problem. I set up tools that make jobs smaller, and I think about that more than I admit.

headlineQuote: I set up tools that make jobs smaller, and I think about that more than I admit.
portrait: Emeka is a 27-year-old on the **new-homes desk**, selling from a show home on a new estate.
He uses **AI every day** and built his own lead tracker.
He's pragmatic, explains AI to his mates, and runs a small **video side business**.
He feels safe in slower pictures but **alarmed** when AGI arrives in 2028.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because his **AI skills** stop counting and he has three weeks saved.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid training** in hands-on work like electrics for people his age.
**Honesty** from the developer about the estate.
